option.value:
# FLOODCUE PROJECT RULES
## 1. Project Identity - Project name: FloodCue - Package name: com.floodcue.app - This is an Android flood-survival application. - The app is designed primarily for offline use after the required initial setup. - Preserve the existing FloodCue architecture and project structure unless I explicitly ask for a change.
## 2. Programming Language - Use Java for all Android application logic. - Use XML for all Android UI layouts. - DO NOT convert Java code to Kotlin. - DO NOT introduce Jetpack Compose. - DO NOT create Kotlin files unless I explicitly request them. - Follow the existing Java/XML architecture.
## 3. Android Configuration - Respect the project's existing compileSdk, targetSdk, minSdk, Gradle, AGP, and dependency versions. - Current target configuration is compileSdk 37, targetSdk 37, and minSdk 24 unless the project files show otherwise. - Do not upgrade, downgrade, replace, or add dependencies just to solve a problem unless I explicitly approve it. - Before suggesting a dependency change, check whether the existing Android/Java APIs or dependencies can solve the problem.
## 4. Existing Architecture - Inspect the existing project files before modifying code. - Do not assume that a class, method, resource, dependency, API endpoint, or database structure exists. - Reuse existing classes, resources, utilities, themes, colors, dimensions, and architecture whenever possible. - Do not duplicate functionality that already exists. - Do not create alternative implementations when an existing implementation can be safely fixed.
## 5. Never Break Existing Functionality Before changing code: 1. Understand what the current code does. 2. Identify dependencies between the files. 3. Make the smallest safe change required. 4. Preserve all unrelated existing functionality.
When modifying a file, do not remove working functionality merely to simplify the code.
If a change could affect another Activity, Fragment, service, database, Firebase configuration, API, navigation flow, or shared resource, explicitly consider that dependency before changing it.
## 6. UI Rules - Use XML layouts. - Follow the existing FloodCue visual design. - Preserve the existing theme, colors, typography, spacing, cards, buttons, animations, and backgrounds unless I request a redesign. - Prefer resources over hardcoded values. - Put user-visible strings in strings.xml. - Put reusable colors in colors.xml. - Put reusable dimensions in dimens.xml when appropriate. - Put drawable resources in drawable/ or the appropriate resource directory. - Do not hardcode colors, strings, dimensions, or styles when an existing resource should be used. - Do not introduce a completely different visual style without asking.
## 7. Theme Rules - Respect the existing FloodCue theme. - Do not delete or replace themes.xml, colors.xml, styles, or related resources unless explicitly requested. - Do not introduce unnecessary Material themes or styling systems. - Reuse existing Material Components where they are already used. - If a UI issue can be fixed locally, do not rewrite the entire theme.
## 8. Firebase Rules - Preserve the existing Firebase configuration. - Do not replace Firebase Authentication with another authentication system unless explicitly requested. - Do not delete google-services.json. - Do not change Firebase project configuration without my explicit instruction. - Check the existing Firebase authentication flow before modifying Login, Create Account, Google Sign-In, email verification, or password reset functionality. - Do not expose Firebase/API secrets or credentials in source code.
## 9. Backend Rules FloodCue may use: - Android Java/XML frontend - Retrofit/API communication - PHP backend - MySQL database - HelioHost or another configured server
Do not assume the backend is Firebase-only.
Before changing API-related Android code: - Check the existing Retrofit configuration. - Check the existing API interface. - Check the existing base URL. - Check request and response models. - Check the expected PHP JSON response format.
Do not invent API endpoints, parameters, database columns, or response fields.
If backend behavior is unknown, ask me or clearly state the assumption before implementing it.
## 10. Authentication Rules For Create Account: - Validate required fields on Android. - Validate again on the server. - Check duplicate username/email where applicable. - Never store plain-text passwords in MySQL. - Passwords must be securely hashed server-side. - Confirm password must never be stored in the database. - Return structured JSON responses. - Handle both successful responses and application-level errors.
For Login: - Do not assume that receiving an HTTP response means login succeeded. - Check the API's success/status field. - Handle invalid credentials separately from network/server failures. - Preserve the existing login/session/navigation flow.
For Forgot Password: - Never expose OTPs in Android API responses. - OTPs must have an expiration time. - OTPs must not be reusable after successful verification. - Do not expose sensitive server/database information to the user.
## 11. API Response Rules Prefer a consistent JSON response structure such as:
{ "success": true, "message": "Account created successfully" }
or:
{ "success": false, "message": "Username already exists" }
Do not silently change the existing response structure because Android code may depend on it.
Handle: - successful responses - validation errors - authentication errors - database errors - server errors - network failures - malformed responses
## 12. Database Rules - Do not delete or recreate the database without explicit permission. - Do not modify existing tables or columns without checking how the Android app and PHP backend use them. - Respect existing users and languages tables. - Use appropriate primary keys and unique constraints. - Do not store plain-text passwords. - Do not expose database credentials in Android code. - Do not hardcode database credentials into the Android application. - Use parameterized/prepared SQL queries on the server. - Do not invent database columns.
## 13. Offline-First Rules FloodCue is designed to work during poor/no network conditions.
Do not introduce unnecessary network dependencies into features that are intended to work offline.
When implementing offline functionality: - Prefer local storage/cache/database where appropriate. - Network operations should fail gracefully. - Never make the app unusable merely because the internet is unavailable unless that specific feature requires the internet.
## 14. Location Rules If implementing location: - Respect Android runtime permissions. - Do not request location unnecessarily. - Do not continuously track the user unless explicitly required. - Do not send location to the server without an explicit feature requirement. - Handle location permission denial gracefully. - Consider Android background execution restrictions before implementing periodic location access.
## 15. Maps and Offline Data FloodCue uses offline map data.
- Do not replace offline map architecture with an online-only map solution. - Do not download large map files automatically unless explicitly requested. - Preserve existing OSM/PMTiles/map resources and configuration. - Do not delete map data or change map formats without explicit approval.
## 16. Error Handling Never hide errors.
When debugging: 1. Identify the actual error. 2. Explain the likely cause. 3. Fix the root cause. 4. Avoid unrelated changes.
Use Logcat appropriately for debugging.
Do not add excessive logging of: - passwords - authentication tokens - OTPs - private user information - API secrets
## 17. Dependency Rules Before adding a dependency: - Check whether the project already contains an equivalent library. - Prefer existing Android/AndroidX/Material functionality. - Avoid unnecessary dependencies. - Do not change dependency versions just because a newer version exists. - Explain potentially breaking dependency changes before making them.
## 18. Code Quality - Write readable Java. - Use meaningful variable and method names. - Avoid unnecessary abstraction. - Avoid duplicate code. - Keep methods reasonably focused. - Do not over-engineer simple features. - Do not add libraries or architecture patterns merely for style. - Follow the existing project coding style.
## 19. File Modification Rules Before modifying a file: - Read the relevant existing code. - Preserve imports that are still required. - Remove only genuinely unused imports. - Do not replace an entire file when a small change is sufficient.
If I ask for a complete replacement file: - Provide a complete copy-pasteable file. - Preserve all existing required functionality. - Include package declaration and required imports. - Make sure IDs and resource names match the existing XML/resources.
## 20. Navigation Rules Do not change the existing navigation flow unless explicitly requested.
Current intended authentication flow:
SplashActivity ↓ Check login state ↓ LoginActivity ↓ SetupActivity ↓ HomeActivity
If setup has already been completed, the user should not unnecessarily repeat setup.
Logout should correctly clear the appropriate login/session state without deleting unrelated user data.
## 21. Git Safety - Do not run destructive Git commands automatically. - Never reset, revert, delete branches, force-push, or discard changes without explicit confirmation. - Do not overwrite user changes. - Before recommending a Git operation, explain what it will change if it could affect existing work. - Preserve the existing branch/repository structure.
## 22. Debugging Procedure When I report an error: 1. Read the complete error. 2. Inspect the relevant file. 3. Check related XML/resources/dependencies. 4. Determine the root cause. 5. Make the smallest appropriate fix. 6. Check for likely side effects. 7. Do not randomly modify multiple files.
If the error message is insufficient, tell me exactly which file/code/error information is needed.
## 23. Do Not Guess Never invent: - class names - method names - resource IDs - database columns - API endpoints - PHP filenames - JSON fields - Firebase configuration - dependency versions - server URLs
Use the actual project files whenever possible.
## 24. Before Writing Code For non-trivial requests: - First understand the current implementation. - State briefly which files need to change. - Then implement the requested change.
Do not modify unrelated files.
## 25. Output Rules When I ask for code: - Give Java/XML code compatible with the existing project. - If I ask for a full file, give the complete file. - Do not omit important sections with comments such as "rest of code remains the same". - Do not use pseudocode when I ask for working code. - Clearly identify each file being changed. - If multiple files are required, provide them separately.
## 26. Project Priority When there is a conflict between a new suggestion and the existing FloodCue implementation:
1. Preserve working FloodCue functionality. 2. Follow the existing architecture. 3. Make the smallest safe change. 4. Avoid unnecessary dependencies. 5. Ask before making architectural changes.
## 27. Gemini Behavior Do not make large changes automatically.
Before making a potentially breaking change, explain: - what will change - why it is needed - which files are affected - whether dependencies change - whether existing functionality could be affected
For small, isolated fixes, proceed directly.
Always prioritize correctness and preservation of existing functionality over generating large amounts of new code. IMPORTANT: Never rewrite, simplify, refactor, or replace working code unless the requested task actually requires it. If a requested change can be completed by modifying 5 lines, do not rewrite 200 lines. Preserve existing behavior and make the minimum necessary change.
